title: EVALUATION OF YOUTUBE CONTENT REGARDING VARENICLINE AND SMOKING CESSATION
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of YouTube videos on varenicline/smoking cessation. Two public health specialists classified each video as useful or misleading against an explicit veracity definition, and the paper reports the share of items classified misleading with a stated denominator (31 of 142, 22% in the Abstract and Tables 4-5; 34 of 144, 23.6% in the Results narrative). This meets the CONTENT criterion (share of items in a sample classified misleading/false).

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language YouTube videos, no country restriction; study run in Turkey)
estimates.date: Search and data recording performed 6 March 2021
estimates.measure_type: % of English-language YouTube videos on varenicline/smoking cessation classified as containing misleading information
estimates.value_raw: Of the videos evaluated, 78% were classified as useful, while the remaining 22% were misleading (Abstract); Table 4 gives Total (n=142) (100%), Useful (n=111) (78%), Misleading (n=31) (22%)
estimates.denominator: 142 English-language videos in the analytic sample (Tables 4 and 5), drawn from the 360 videos taken from the first three pages of view-count-sorted results for six search terms after removing duplicates, non-English, irrelevant, over-40-minute and poor-sound videos (the Results narrative says 144 videos remained)
estimates.definition: A video was 'misleading' if it contained information that has not been proven scientifically or that has been scientifically proven to be wrong under any of the study's content subheadings (usage, side effects, efficacy, mechanism, harms of addiction, psychology of addiction, safety of the active substance, referral to professional help)
estimates.misinfo_def: Misleading videos were considered any video containing information that has not been proven scientifically or that has been scientifically proven to be wrong under any of the topics mentioned above.
estimates.source_quote: Of the videos evaluated, 78% were classified as useful, while the remaining 22% were mislead-
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, p. 37 (line-broken as 'mislead-/ing'); Table 4, p. 41. The Results narrative on p. 40 instead reports 'Misleading information was determined in 34 videos (23.6%)'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two public health specialists evaluated every video independently. Reported inter-rater agreement (Cohen's Kappa 0.81 for GQS and 0.84 for the modified DISCERN tool) is for the two quality instruments; no separate kappa is reported for the useful/misleading classification. The authors flag the ratings as 'subjective interpretations of the persons that evaluated the videos'.
estimates.moderator_quote: We searched on YouTube using the following key terms: varenicline, smoking cessation varenicline, quit smoking varenicline, smoking cessation medicine, quit smoking medicine, and medication to quit smoking. Only English videos were included in the study. ... Video listings are made based on view counts. ... Therefore, 360 videos were selected from the six search terms. Following the elimination of videos according to the defined criteria, 144 videos were selected for evaluation.
estimates.notes: The paper is internally inconsistent about this value. The Abstract, Table 4 and Table 5 all give 31 misleading videos of 142 (22%), with 111 useful (78%); the Results narrative instead gives 'Misleading information was determined in 34 videos (23.6%)' over the 144 videos its flow description reports. The 22% (31/142) figure is kept because it is the one the paper puts in its abstract, in both tables and in the analytic samples actually used for the group comparisons (useful n=111 vs misleading n=31); the 23.6% (34/144) variant is recorded here rather than as a second row because it is the same estimate reported inconsistently, not a distinct estimate. Confidence is medium for that reason. Table 4 also contains obvious typographical errors (health facility 1/19 labelled 4.3%, pharmacy company 0 labelled 100%). The source_quote stops at the Abstract's hyphenated line break ('mislead-/ing'), which is where the contiguous verbatim span ends. All six search terms concern one issue (smoking-cessation medication), and the corpus is rank-truncated to the first three pages by view count, hence denom_scope topical with denom_selection curated.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) the 78% 'useful' share — the complement of the misleading share; (2) the modified DISCERN and Global Quality Scale scores (useful 2.6+/-1.1 and 2.7+/-1.1; misleading 1.3+/-0.7 and 1.5+/-0.6) — quality instruments reported as means only, so no share and no row; (3) the misleading share by uploader source in Table 4 (independent users 6/7 = 85.7%; agencies/TV channels 14/14 = 100%; consumers 9/61 = 14.8%; doctors 1/11 = 9.1%; health facilities 1/19 = 4.3%; academic institutions and pharmacy companies 0%) — subgroup rows, not the paper's headline; (4) the topic-coverage frequencies in Table 3 (side effects 76.6%, effectiveness 62.1%, etc.) — coverage, not veracity. Main uncertainty: the numerator/denominator inconsistency between the Results (34/144, 23.6%) and the Abstract/Tables (31/142, 22%); Table 4 also carries obvious typographical errors (health facility 1/19 labelled 4.3%, pharmacy company 0 labelled 100%, total n=142 versus 144 in the text).

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis. Search on 6 March 2021 with six terms (varenicline, smoking cessation varenicline, quit smoking varenicline, smoking cessation medicine, quit smoking medicine, medication to quit smoking); results sorted by view count, first three pages taken (360 videos), and duplicates (123), non-English (50), irrelevant (31), over-40-minute (8) and poor-sound (4) videos removed, leaving 144. Two public health specialists rated every video independently on the Global Quality Scale and modified DISCERN and classified it useful or misleading; kappa 0.81 (GQS) and 0.84 (DISCERN). Analyses in SPSS v15 (t-test / Mann-Whitney U / chi-square). Ethical approval not required. Authors note the subjectivity of the ratings and the single-time-point snapshot as limitations.
